title: Mechanical self-replication of a production cell from feedstock

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a production cell that makes and assembles the mechanical equipment of a working successor from specified bar, sheet, wire, and polymer stock. The successor must include the equipment needed to repeat that manufacturing process: cell A produces cell B, and B produces a functioning cell C under the same rules. Reproducing a frame or assembling supplied robot modules would satisfy only part of this goal.

The intended manufacturing boundary includes structural parts, bearings, actuators, tools, and assembly equipment. Pre-made electronic modules may be supplied, so semiconductor fabrication is outside the target. That allowance requires a precise boundary: a supplied controller cannot quietly bring with it the motors, bearings, transmissions, or other mechanical hardware that the cell is supposed to manufacture. External energy, consumables, inherited equipment, and human assistance must also be accounted for.

significance.text: If achieved, repeatable mechanical replication could change how manufacturing capacity expands. A seed installation could produce the mechanical equipment for additional production cells, reducing the need to obtain a separately manufactured set of machines for every expansion. This is a conditional consequence of the proposed capability, rather than an established result.

Remote manufacturing is a plausible downstream application: shipping a seed cell and suitable supplies could eventually support local production of further equipment. Its value would depend on feedstock availability and preparation, energy, supplied electronics, transport, maintenance, and the ability to operate reliably in the destination environment. Replication would not itself establish independence from industrial supply chains.

The analogy to biological reproduction or automatically multiplying factories has important limits. Producing two successive generations would not establish rapid growth, competitive cost, indefinite replication, or sustained reliability. Capacity growth would also depend on replication time, material yield, tool replacement, and how much output must be devoted to maintaining existing cells. These are separate performance questions that a successful mechanical replication demonstration would make possible to investigate.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central missing capability is closure of the specified mechanical manufacturing loop: a cell must manufacture and assemble all the mechanical equipment its successor needs to do the same. The supplied research identifies dependence on externally manufactured components as the obstacle, but does not provide inspectable evidence establishing the present extent of that dependence across the field. The engineering target remains coherent despite that evidentiary limitation.

As an engineering analysis of the proposal, the difficult integration spans materials processing, precision fabrication, robotic handling, assembly, metrology, and control. Producing individual parts is insufficient if the resulting cell cannot align, join, calibrate, and operate them. Bearings and actuators must meet functional requirements; the successor's tools must be capable of making another generation of those same parts. The permitted stock forms and material specifications therefore matter as much as the final machine design.

A further barrier is preserving capability across generations. Dimensional deviations, assembly errors, calibration drift, tool wear, and changes in actuator performance could accumulate or undermine replication. A convincing system would need ways to measure and correct these changes, replace worn tooling within the declared boundary, and avoid relying on undeclared inherited fixtures or precision equipment. These are proposed engineering requirements, not claims of experimentally established failure mechanisms in a particular machine.

current_state.text: The supplied research reports self-reconfiguring modular robots and partial machine replication as existing lines of work. Its sole reference is Matthew S. Moses and Gregory S. Chirikjian's 2020 review, “Robotic Self-Replication.” However, the supplied source index retains no document artifact or source passage, and the accessible journal record described in the research did not expose the relevant full text. The reported achievements therefore cannot be independently assessed for their dates, experimental scope, or manufacturing boundaries from these inputs.

The first-pass research specifically attributed to that review a discussion of printers relying on externally produced nozzles, extruders, and motors. Because the passage was not exposed in the supplied check, those examples should remain a reported attribution rather than a verified inventory of current limitations. The extraction gap is not evidence that the attributed discussion or the underlying results are false.

The distinction between these research directions and the proposed target is substantive. Modular reconfiguration rearranges existing modules; partial replication reproduces some components or capabilities. Neither description alone establishes that a cell manufactures and assembles every mechanical component and tool needed by a successor that can repeat the process. Supplied electronics would remain permissible within this proposal, making it narrower than complete self-reproduction.

No inspectable demonstration of the proposed A-to-B-to-C capability is supplied. The review also had no bounded search results or populated freshness record with which to assess the field as of November 1, 2026. Consequently, these inputs establish neither that the full target has been achieved nor that it remains open today. They provide no assessable quantitative replication performance, later demonstration, preprint result, or disputed experimental result.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: declare the allowed bar, sheet, wire, and polymer stock, then have cell A fabricate and assemble every structural part, bearing, actuator, and tool required for a functioning cell B, including B's replication equipment. Have B fabricate and assemble a functioning cell C under the same input and assistance rules. Both successors should be independently tested against predefined manufacturing, assembly, and functional acceptance criteria.
completion_criteria.label: Complete functioning mechanical successors fabricated and assembled across two generations

completion_criteria.text: The demonstration should specify the boundary between supplied electronic modules and mechanical actuator hardware, list the quantities and contents of all supplied modules, and disclose external energy, consumables, inherited equipment, and every human intervention. Tooling and fixtures need explicit accounting, including whether they are reproduced, consumed, transferred from the parent, or supplied externally. Otherwise, an apparently complete successor could depend on mechanical inputs omitted from the claimed boundary.
completion_criteria.label: Full accounting of supplied modules, mechanical boundaries, and external dependencies

completion_criteria.text: Proposed acceptance evidence should include dimensional errors, assembly success, calibration results, functional performance, and changes from A to B to C. The tests should show that B possesses the manufacturing capability required to produce C, alongside evidence that both offspring perform their intended production functions. No numerical tolerances or performance thresholds are established by the supplied material; those should be selected and justified for the declared cell design.
completion_criteria.label: Acceptance tests establish offspring production functions and B’s replication capability

completion_criteria.text: For reproducibility, the design, input specifications, control procedures, intervention record, and measurement methods should be documented sufficiently for an independent team to repeat the demonstration. Replication time, energy and material use, yield, tool consumption, and maintenance requirements would define its practical boundaries. Two successive generations would demonstrate the specified capability over that tested span; broader trials would establish greater demonstrated breadth, without proving indefinite replication or universal applicability.
completion_criteria.label: Documentation enables independent repetition and defines tested practical boundaries

related_concepts.text: MEC-13, “General-purpose synthesis of practical mechanisms,” overlaps in turning functional requirements into manufacturable mechanisms. MEC-09 adds the requirement that a production cell reproduce its own mechanical manufacturing capability. MEC-06, “Macroscopic atomically precise mechanosynthesis,” concerns a different fabrication capability and precision regime; the proposed stock-based replication target does not require atomic precision.

MEC-05, “Programmable solids that become different load-bearing mechanisms,” and MEC-10, “Stress-directed growth of load-bearing structures,” offer conceptual connections through reconfiguration and formation of useful structures. Changing an existing structure's configuration or growing a load-bearing form does not by itself reproduce a cell's bearings, actuators, tooling, and assembly capability.

MEC-08, “Distributed actuators that simultaneously match skeletal muscle,” overlaps through actuation, but MEC-09 requires reproducible actuators adequate for the cell's tasks rather than muscle-matching performance. MEC-02, “Service-life superlubricity in ordinary machine contacts,” MEC-11, “Transferable prediction of wear and component life,” and MEC-12, “Predictive mechanics of real, evolving surface contacts,” could help address friction, wear, and precision retention. These connections concern possible enabling capabilities, not prerequisites established by the supplied evidence.

MEC-04, “Ambient fatigue immunity in bulk structural metals,” and MEC-07, “Bulk structural solids at a large fraction of ideal strength,” concern material durability and strength that could improve a cell's lifetime or design. MEC-09 would still require manufacturing and assembly closure using its declared materials. MEC-01, “An engineering-predictive theory of turbulent flow,” MEC-03, “Engines that make sub-100 °C heat worth converting,” and MEC-14, “Low-cost mechanical storage with high efficiency over long periods,” have more indirect connections through process design or energy infrastructure; none substitutes for the replication capability.

change_log.change: Preserved MEC-09's identity and mechanical scope while explicitly including the successor's replication equipment.
change_log.reason: A functioning machine copy is insufficient unless it can manufacture and assemble the next generation.

change_log.change: Expanded the proposed demonstration to define electronic-module boundaries, mechanical actuator hardware, inherited equipment, tooling, and human assistance.
change_log.reason: These distinctions prevent undeclared mechanical inputs from creating apparent manufacturing closure.

change_log.change: Added independent functional acceptance criteria and measurements of dimensional and performance changes across generations.
change_log.reason: The review identified these as necessary to make replication capability and error control testable.

change_log.change: Qualified reports of modular robots, partial replication, and externally supplied printer components while retaining their explanatory role.
change_log.reason: The sole reference lacks retained artifacts and exposed supporting passages; this limits verification without disproving the reported work.

change_log.change: Separated conditional capacity expansion from economic scaling, remote utility, and indefinite sustainability.
change_log.reason: Those downstream outcomes require evidence beyond a successful two-generation demonstration.

change_log.change: Preserved the review's freshness and access limitations without assigning an overall negative verdict to the concept.
change_log.reason: The supplied evidence cannot establish the present-day achievement or openness of the full target.

change_log.change: Explained relationships to the supplied roster as conceptual synthesis.
change_log.reason: Relevant enabling capabilities and adjacent goals should remain distinct innovations rather than being merged into mechanical replication.

unresolved_issues: The contents and completeness of the cited 2020 review remain unverified from the supplied record; no retained artifact or relevant passage is available.
The field's status as of November 1, 2026, and any subsequent demonstrations are unassessed because the supplied freshness record and bounded search results are absent.
The allowed stock specifications, electronic-module contents, actuator boundary, consumables, and rules for inherited tooling remain to be defined.
No cell design, numerical acceptance tolerances, replication time, resource budget, or economic target is supplied.
Longer-term error control, maintenance closure, and sustained replication would require demonstrations beyond the proposed two-generation test.

brief.title: Machines that build working copies of themselves
possible: A manufacturer could expand a workshop by having its machines build another working set from bars, sheets, wire and polymer stock. The new set would then build a further working set under the same rules.
Each copy would make and assemble all the mechanical equipment needed to repeat the process, including motors, bearings and tools. Ready-made electronics could be supplied.
why: Manufacturing capacity could grow from a seed installation, reducing the need to buy a separately manufactured set of machines for every expansion.
Remote communities and operations could use a seed workshop and suitable supplies to produce more equipment locally.

sources.who: Matthew S. Moses and Gregory S. Chirikjian
sources.showed: This review discusses robots that rearrange existing modules and machines that reproduce some of their own components.
sources.cited_for: It describes research directions toward machines that reproduce themselves.
sources.not_established: Partial reproduction and rearranging existing modules do not establish a complete mechanical manufacturing loop.

sources.showed: Sells reported making parts that were assembled into a working copy of a printer. The copy then successfully made one of its own parts.
sources.quote:
Self-manufacture was demons trated by assembling this set of parts 
into a working copy of the original machine.
sources.cited_for: A working successor could retain the ability to manufacture a component of itself.
sources.not_established: This did not establish manufacture and assembly of every mechanical component and tool needed for successive complete copies.

sources.who: Alex Ellery, Abdurr Elaskri, Mariappan Parans Paranthaman and Fabrice Bernier
sources.showed: The researchers printed parts in successive layers and assembled them by hand into a working electric motor. Performance was poor because of limitations in the wire coils.
sources.quote:
We have
demonstrated that DC electric motors can be 3D printed and assembled into a functional
system.
sources.cited_for: Making a working motor addresses a component that a mechanically reproducing workshop would need.
sources.not_established: The motor required hand assembly and did not demonstrate an integrated workshop capable of reproducing itself.

shown: Edward Anthony Sells reported a printer making parts for a working copy, which then made one of its own parts. This demonstrated partial reproduction with a successor that retained a manufacturing function.
Alex Ellery and colleagues made a working electric motor from printed parts. They assembled it by hand, and its performance was poor because of the wire coils.
missing: A complete workshop must make and assemble every mechanical component and tool its successor needs to repeat the process.
A successor must build a further functioning workshop under the same rules for materials, supplied equipment and human help.
Measurements must establish that successors retain their production abilities and can correct errors and replace worn tools.
An independent team must repeat the demonstration with clearly defined inputs and measured resource use.

milestones.label: Complete working successors across two generations
milestones.explanation: A workshop would have to make and assemble a working successor that builds another under the same rules. This would demonstrate that the mechanical manufacturing loop repeats.

milestones.label: All supplied equipment and outside help accounted for
milestones.explanation: The demonstration would have to account for supplied electronics, mechanical hardware, tools, energy, consumables and human help. This would establish which equipment the workshop actually reproduces.

milestones.label: Successors pass tests of production and copying ability
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to measure accuracy, assembly, adjustment and performance across generations, including the successor’s ability to build another. This would establish that the copies retain the required manufacturing functions.

milestones.label: Independent repetition with measured practical limits
milestones.explanation: An independent team would have to repeat the work using documented designs and procedures, while measuring time, resources and maintenance. This would establish reproducibility and the tested practical limits.

uncertain: The permitted stock, contents of supplied electronics and rules for inherited tools still need precise definitions.
Required accuracy and performance thresholds depend on the workshop design and remain to be justified.
Success across the tested generations would leave long-term reliability, maintenance needs and competitive cost unresolved.

page.title: Mechanical self-replication from industrial feedstock
page.definition: A production cell manufactures and assembles all the mechanical equipment of a working successor from industrial stock; that successor repeats the process. This requires mechanical parts closure: every structural part, bearing, actuator, transmission, tool and fixture needed for replication is reproduced, while declared electronic modules and external energy may be supplied.

goal.need: Making successor parts leaves assembly and externally manufactured equipment to be supplied. In one RepRap demonstration reported in January 2009, printing the parts took approximately 100 hours and manual assembly approximately 20 hours; motors and other components were imported. NASA’s replicating-factory study identifies expansion from a seed installation as an application. Mechanical replication addresses the manufacture and assembly of the production equipment itself.

statements.quote: It was designed to make its own parts to be assembled by people into another RepRap.
statements.context: The published goal allows human assembly and externally supplied components.

completion.title: A production cell makes a mechanical successor that makes another under identical input rules.
completion.criterion: Cell A manufactures and assembles operational cell B, and B manufactures and assembles operational cell C, from declared bar, sheet, wire and polymer stock. Each successor contains all mechanical structures, bearings, actuators, transmissions, fabrication tools, fixtures and assembly equipment needed to repeat the process. Supplied electronic modules contain none of that mechanical equipment. Energy and declared process consumables may be supplied; no mechanical equipment is imported or transferred between cells. People do not fabricate, assemble or calibrate the successors. B and C meet the declared machine specifications.
completion.set_by: Atlas; restricted mechanical version of the published replication and parts-closure goals.
completion.basis: Searches of NASA replication studies, RepRap validation criteria, ISO robotics standards and proposed constructor-prize rules found no adopted test combining industrial stock, two successive generations and an electronics-only component exception. NASA specifies two-generation robotic assembly; RepRap distinguishes manufacture from assembly. The test combines those requirements within the stated mechanical boundary.

milestones.title: A printer manufactures the printed parts for a working copy of itself.
milestones.criterion: A parent printer manufactures the designated printable component set for a functioning child; the project's listed imported components and manual assembly are allowed. Sells reports one working parent–child pair. The child manufactured its first successful grandchild part on 29 May 2008 at 14:00 UTC. This result establishes partial manufacture and retained printing capability.
milestones.set_by: RepRap project, validation criterion in Sells’s thesis, §3.4; imported-component boundary in §3.1.
milestones.threshold_quote: To prove self-replication the parent must manufacture a child.

milestones.title: Fabricated motor components operate together as a DC electric motor.
milestones.criterion: Fabricated magnetic, structural and winding components are assembled into a motor that produces rotation under electrical power. Ellery and colleagues reported a hand-assembled printed motor on 1 August 2025; its reported speed plateaued at 700 revolutions per minute. A preprint posted on 13 October 2025 also reports printed actuators and control elements. That preprint is not peer reviewed and reports component tests rather than successive production cells.
milestones.set_by: Ellery and colleagues, published motor-fabrication experiments in Machines, §2; a component demonstration for their self-replication research.
milestones.threshold_quote: We have demonstrated that DC electric motors can be 3D printed and assembled into a functional system.

milestones.title: A robot assembles a successor that assembles another successor from supplied parts.
milestones.criterion: A construction robot reproduces itself and its necessary peripheral equipment, including the logic system, over two generations, producing one replica in each generation. Parts, subassemblies and initially supplied assembly aids are permitted. Related experimental evidence published on 12 May 2005 includes a four-module robot assembling a copy in approximately 2.5 minutes from supplied 10-centimetre cubes, manually replenished at two feeding locations.
milestones.set_by: NASA Marshall Space Flight Center, NASA TM-78304, §8.5.1, demonstration phase a.
milestones.threshold_quote: including the logic system over two generations

milestones.title: Robots assemble operating machines that manufacture robot parts.
milestones.criterion: Manipulators assemble parts-producing machinery, such as a gear-manufacturing machine, and that machinery makes parts. This is the fabrication-equipment step in NASA’s middle-out development scheme. The scheme subsequently requires the enlarged population of machines to produce its complete parts inventory.
milestones.set_by: NASA/ASEE Replicating Systems Concepts Team, Advanced Automation for Space Missions, §5.6.4, stage 3; a proposed development scheme.
milestones.threshold_quote: are used to build the machines which make the parts.

milestones.title: A production cell manufactures and assembles one complete mechanical successor from stock.
milestones.criterion: Cell A produces operational cell B under the completion test’s stock, electronics, consumables and human-assistance rules. B includes every mechanical component, tool, fixture and assembly device required to reproduce the cell and meets its declared specifications. B’s manufacture of cell C remains to be demonstrated.
milestones.set_by: Atlas; the single-generation precursor to completion. Searches of NASA and RepRap criteria found no published test with this exact mechanical boundary and supplied-electronics exception.

not_found: No adopted external completion test was found for the exact mechanical boundary with supplied electronics.
No demonstration satisfying the complete mechanical successor criterion or the two-generation feedstock criterion was identified.
No qualifying demonstration of NASA’s robot-assembled parts-producing machinery stage was identified.
